newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia TRI streamlining draws mixed reactions.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia TRI streamlining draws mixed reactions.

text.p: Technology Resources Industries Bhd's (TRI) breakup into seven companies will help it face intense competition in Malaysia and smooth its partnership with Germany's Deutsche Telekom, analysts said on Wednesday.

The streamlining plan, announced last weekend by TRI Chairman Tajudin Ramli, was needed to keep the company attractive to investors even if it does not enhance profitablitiy in the short run, they said.
Tajudin announced the company would be split into units concentrating on mobile, fixed-line telecommunications, multimedia services, international ventures and related telecommunications activities.
Malaysia's first and largest mobile phone provider, Celcom, is TRI's main source of income, providing the bulk of the group's pre-tax profits for 1995.
"TRI is trying to convert the group's structure from a vertical one to a horizontal one," said Phua Lee Kerk, telecommunications analyst at Vickers Ballas.
"TRI is currently losing out to the competition because of network capacity constraints and an inferior marketing strategy," Phua said.

Six companies have been given licenses to operate fixed and mobile services in Malaysia, which has a population of 20 million. Celcom's analogue ART 900 service is close to saturation and its digital GSM service lacks national coverage.
A key factor in the restructuring was to facilitate the group's tie-up with Germany's Deutsche Telekom, analysts said.
In June, Deutsche Telekom signed an agreement to acquire one-fifth of TRI for 1.42 billion ringgit ($570 million).

"TRI's vertical structure had been a sticking point in the negotiations with Deutsche Telekom," an analyst at HG Asia said. "So it's not a surprise the restructuring was announced. This will now smooth the way for the deal to go through."
Under the deal, Deutsche Telekom will develop TRI's proposed fixed line services and so does not want the mobile operations to "cloud the issue", the analyst said.
TRI plans to lay fibre-optic cables along existing gas and electricity lines.

Other operators like Binariang, Time Engineering unit Time Telecom and Mutiara Telecommunications are also laying fibre-optic networks, along with Telekom Malaysia, the national telecommunications utility.
The effect of the restructuring on TRI's profitability, is still being queried. "The streamlining is a good idea, but is not too exciting," said the HG Asia analyst.

"Celcom was getting too big to manage efficiently but I can't see how the restructuring is going to benefit the group in the short-term," said Haizan Khir Johari, telecommunications analyst at Schroders Research.
"Celcom is a cash cow, but the rest of the operations have a very long time to go before they bring in any revenue."
Haizan said he was not convinced the restructuring would solve fundamental problems with TRI's long-term strategy.
"Even if 60 percent of the population use things like real-time video-conferencing facilities, only around two to five percent of the total bandwidth of the networks will be utilised."
Bandwidth is the amount of digitised data that can be transferred along a cable in one second. Fibre-optic cables carry vastly more data than traditional copper cables.

"Their strategy and focus is there, but with up to five operators with similar roll-out programmes scheduled for the next four years, it almost seems as if TRI is embarking on these projects simply because it feels it has to," Haizan said.
